items.title: Native backend mints the hidden `Owner` parameter per function, not per instance: a static `MaybeSignal` argument through a generic function is refused natively
items.discussion: found by lane ui-p3b (Order 58, 2026-11-12) while trying `std::ui` on `MaybeSignal`; the lane labelled it F36 in the tree (an archived id), relabelled F168 at the merge; it is why `std::ui` keeps `Bindable<T>` after B737
items.body: The context pass mints a hidden `Owner` parameter on a FUNCTION when one candidate of a dispatch inside it reads the owner (`MaybeSignal`'s reactive arm does). The instance a STATIC argument selects then declares the parameter too, and a caller with no owner threads none. The checker resolves the site per call (B737) and accepts the program; JavaScript passes `undefined`; the native emitter refuses the call by name. With `std::ui` switched to `MaybeSignal` the lane saw the counter example, a one-line `row().gap(dp(8))` and `layout(..)` all refused natively: every tree, static ones included, would have to be built under `comp` or `mount_root`. Repro and pin: `native_differential`'s `#[ignore]`d `f168_a_static_maybe_signal_through_a_generic_needs_no_owner_on_both_backends` (fails natively, passes on JS); `inference::std_surface`'s `ui_r9_a_bound_tree_needs_no_owner_at_the_top_of_main`. Fix: instances carry their own context needs (mint per monomorphic instance, by the per-entry refinement B737 already computes). After it, `std::ui` can move to `MaybeSignal`, and the owner rules on the one remaining difference: a binding with no ambient owner refused (`MaybeSignal`) or kept by its source (`Bindable`).

items.title: gfx host on X11: an input event is sometimes left unread until the next X event (about 1 run in 5 of a release build under xvfb with software Vulkan)
items.kind: bug (native runtime; gfx host event loop)
items.discussion: found by lane ui-p3b (Order 58, 2026-11-12) while measuring the 10,000-row list; predates the lane; not seen in the debug end-to-end tests, but `ui_interaction.rs`'s key steps could flake on CI
items.area: crates/vilan-rt-gfx/src/host (the winit loop), winit 0.30 X11 backend, Mesa's X11 present path
items.body: Observed: an injected key, or the window close, produces no turn; the program sits in `epoll_wait` with the event already sent, and a later pointer move delivers the stuck event. HYPOTHESIS, not proven: Mesa's X11 present path (possibly on its own queue thread) reads the shared X connection, so events land in the client-side queue while winit waits on a socket that is no longer readable. First step: prove or refute it (strace or a counter on wake reasons; check whether the stuck event is in Xlib's queue; try a present mode with no WSI thread). Candidate fixes, in order of preference: wake the loop once shortly after each present so the queue is drained (a bounded `WaitUntil`, back to `Wait` after); a low-rate idle wake while a window is open; an upstream winit report. Exit: 200 runs of the release list example with injected keys lose none; a pin if one can be made deterministic. Check a real GPU and Wayland separately: the hypothesis says they may not share the defect.

items.title: `std::ui` keeps each element's scene in window coordinates, so an insert or a removal rebuilds the scene of every element below it (30,000 scenes for a 10,000-row list)
items.discussion: measured by lane ui-p3b (Order 58, 2026-11-12): insert at top 14.1 ms layout / 7.9 ms paint, remove 14.8 / 8.7, move bottom to top 9.4 / 10.2 (release, medians of 7, software Vulkan under xvfb); a one-row change is 3.5 / 0.8
items.body: Every row below an insert or removal gets a new box, and because a cached scene holds window coordinates it is rebuilt. Keep each element's scene in its own coordinates and place it under a translate: a moved element then keeps its scene and the paint cost of a list operation is close to constant. Layout's share (taffy re-placing 10,000 cached siblings, 30,000 moved boxes) is separate and goes with P4's virtual list. Check clips and scroll offsets, which already translate, and the hit test, which reads boxes not scenes.
